name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q01 - Three critical research areas of biotechnology

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the three critical research areas of biotechnology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biotechnology deals with the industrial-scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants, and animals.

Step 2: Evaluation
The three critical research areas of biotechnology are: (1) providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism (usually a microbe or pure enzyme), (2) creating optimal conditions through engineering for a catalyst to act, and (3) downstream processing technologies to purify the protein or organic compound. Conventional cross-breeding of wild varieties in open fields is a traditional agricultural practice rather than one of these three critical biotechnology research areas.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Conventional cross-breeding of wild crop varieties in open fields is not one of the three critical research areas of biotechnology.

answer.text: Providing the best catalyst in the form of an improved organism or pure enzyme
Creating optimal conditions through engineering for a catalyst to act
Conventional cross-breeding of wild crop varieties in open fields
Downstream processing technologies to purify the protein or organic compound

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q02 - Broad applications of modern biotechnology

questiontext.text: Which set of applications correctly represents the scope of modern biotechnology as described in the chapter?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biotechnology uses genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants, and animals for industrial-scale production and environmental and medical applications.

Step 2: Evaluation
The applications of biotechnology include therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops for agriculture, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, and energy production. Plate tectonics, mineral smelting, and astronomical instrumentation are unrelated physical/geological domains.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therapeutics, diagnostics, genetically modified crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, and energy production accurately represent the applications of biotechnology.

answer.text: Therapeutics, diagnostics, GM crops, processed food, bioremediation, waste treatment, and energy production
Therapeutics, mineral smelting, GM crops, processed food, and plate tectonics
Diagnostics, bioremediation, astronomical optics, and energy production
Waste treatment, synthetic polymer moulding, diagnostics, and conventional tillage

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q03 - Green Revolution impact on food supply

questiontext.text: By what factor did the Green Revolution succeed in increasing the food supply, primarily through better management practices and the use of agrochemicals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Green Revolution was a major agricultural transformation aimed at boosting food production using improved crop varieties, better management practices, and agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides).

Step 2: Evaluation
The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply, although even this threefold increase was insufficient to feed the growing human population.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply.

answer.text: Doubling the food supply
Tripling the food supply
Quadrupling the food supply
Tenfold increase in the food supply

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q04 - Definition of Genetically Modified Organisms

questiontext.text: Organisms such as plants, bacteria, fungi, and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic engineering allows the deliberate alteration of an organism's genetic makeup by introducing or modifying specific genes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plants, bacteria, fungi, and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs). Somaclonal variants, wild-type isolates, and somatic hybrids arise through different biological or tissue-culture processes rather than direct gene manipulation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Such organisms are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs).

answer.text: Somaclonal variants
Wild-type isolates
Somatic hybrids
Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q05 - Useful traits introduced in GM plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT an advantage achieved through genetic modification of crop plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic modification has been used to improve crop resilience, reduce chemical inputs, minimise harvest losses, and enhance nutritional quality.

Step 2: Evaluation
GM plants have been made more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat), reduced reliance on chemical pesticides, reduced pest harvest losses, increased efficiency of mineral usage (preventing early exhaustion of soil fertility), and enhanced nutritional value (e.g., golden rice). Genetic modification does not aim to increase dependence on expensive synthetic fertilisers; rather, it improves mineral usage efficiency.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Increasing dependence on expensive synthetic fertilisers is not an advantage of genetic modification.

answer.text: Increased tolerance to abiotic stresses such as cold, drought, salt, and heat
Increased dependence on expensive synthetic chemical fertilisers
Increased efficiency of mineral usage, preventing early exhaustion of soil fertility
Enhanced nutritional value of food, such as Vitamin A-enriched golden rice

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q06 - Golden rice and industrial GM plant products

questiontext.text: Golden rice is a genetically modified crop specifically developed to be enriched with which nutrient, and what additional industrial resources can tailor-made GM plants supply?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Genetic modification can enhance the nutritional profile of staple foods and also repurpose plants into bio-factories for industrial raw materials.

Step 2: Evaluation
Golden rice is Vitamin A-enriched rice, illustrating enhanced nutritional value of food. In addition, GM technology has been used to create tailor-made plants to supply alternative resources to industries in the form of starches, fuels, and pharmaceuticals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Golden rice is enriched with Vitamin A, and tailor-made GM plants supply starches, fuels, and pharmaceuticals to industries.

answer.text: Vitamin C; heavy metals and synthetic plastics
Vitamin D; mineral ores and petrochemicals
Vitamin A; starches, fuels, and pharmaceuticals
Vitamin B12; agrochemicals and synthetic pesticides

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q07 - Rationale for GM crops over conventional agrochemicals

questiontext.text: Why are genetically modified crops considered a necessary alternative to agro-chemical based agriculture, especially for farmers in developing countries?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Conventional agriculture relies heavily on improved varieties, management practices, and agrochemicals (fertilisers and pesticides), which have economic and biological limits.

Step 2: Evaluation
For farmers in the developing world, agrochemicals are often too expensive, and further yield increases with existing varieties are not possible using conventional breeding. Moreover, minimising fertiliser and chemical usage helps reduce their harmful environmental effects, while GM crops with higher mineral usage efficiency prevent early exhaustion of soil fertility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
GM crops are needed because agrochemicals are too expensive for developing-world farmers, conventional breeding cannot push yields further with existing varieties, and reducing chemical use protects the environment.

answer.text: Because organic agriculture completely eliminates all crop pests without any management practices
Because agrochemicals cannot be manufactured outside developing countries
Because conventional breeding increases abiotic stress tolerance faster than genetic engineering
Because agrochemicals are often too expensive, conventional breeding has reached yield limits with existing varieties, and chemical use harms the environment

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q08 - Source of Bt toxin and transgenic crop examples

questiontext.text: The Bt toxin gene cloned into plants such as cotton, corn, rice, tomato, potato, and soyabean to create a bio-pesticide is isolated from:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pest-resistant transgenic crops express a bacterial insecticidal gene that protects them without external insecticide sprays.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bt toxin is produced by the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (abbreviated Bt). Its toxin gene has been cloned from the bacterium and expressed in crops like Bt cotton, Bt corn, rice, tomato, potato, and soyabean.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Bt toxin gene is isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis.

answer.text: Bacillus thuringiensis
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
Escherichia coli
Meloidogyne incognita

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q09 - Insect groups targeted by Bacillus thuringiensis

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly matches the insect orders killed by strains of Bacillus thuringiensis with their examples?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce insecticidal proteins that target specific insect orders.

Step 2: Evaluation
B. thuringiensis proteins kill lepidopterans (such as tobacco budworm and armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), and dipterans (flies and mosquitoes). Beetles are coleopterans, not dipterans; flies and mosquitoes are dipterans, not lepidopterans; tobacco budworm and armyworm are lepidopterans, not coleopterans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairing is: lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).

answer.text: Lepidopterans (flies, mosquitoes), coleopterans (tobacco budworm), dipterans (beetles)
Lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), dipterans (flies, mosquitoes)
Lepidopterans (beetles), coleopterans (armyworm), dipterans (cotton bollworm)
Lepidopterans (mosquitoes), coleopterans (flies), dipterans (tobacco budworm)

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q10 - Why Bt toxin does not kill Bacillus

questiontext.text: Crystals of Bt toxin produced by Bacillus thuringiensis do not kill the bacterium itself because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bacillus thuringiensis forms protein crystals containing a toxic insecticidal protein during a particular phase of growth.

Step 2: Evaluation
Inside the bacterium, the Bt toxin protein exists as an inactive protoxin. Only after an insect ingests the inactive toxin is it converted into an active form due to the alkaline pH of the insect gut, which solubilises the crystals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The toxin does not kill the bacterium because it exists in an inactive protoxin form inside the bacterial cell.

answer.text: The bacterial cell wall is impermeable to all proteins
The bacterium encloses the active toxin inside a lipid-bound vacuole
The toxin exists as an inactive protoxin inside the bacterium
The bacterium synthesises an anti-toxin enzyme that permanently degrades the crystal

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q11 - Mechanism of insect death by activated Bt toxin

questiontext.text: Once converted into its active form in the insect gut, how does the Bt toxin cause the death of the insect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
After ingestion, the alkaline pH of the insect gut solubilises Bt protein crystals and converts the inactive protoxin into active toxin.

Step 2: Evaluation
The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and creates pores in the cell membrane. These pores cause cell swelling and lysis, eventually leading to the death of the insect.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The activated toxin binds to midgut epithelial cells and creates pores that cause cell swelling and lysis.

answer.text: It inhibits DNA replication in the insect's salivary glands
It blocks neural transmission across the insect's central ganglia
It precipitates digestive enzymes in the insect's hindgut
It binds to midgut epithelial cells and creates pores causing cell swelling and lysis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q12 - Specific cry genes for cotton bollworm and corn borer

questiontext.text: Which of the following combinations of cry genes and their target insect pests is completely accurate?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bt toxins are coded by cry genes and exhibit insect-group specificity.

Step 2: Evaluation
The proteins encoded by the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, while the protein encoded by cryIAb controls corn borer.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms, and cryIAb controls corn borer.

answer.text: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; cryIAb controls corn borer
cryIAb and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; cryIAc controls corn borer
cryIAc and cryIAb control corn borer; cryIIAb controls cotton bollworms
cryIIAb controls corn borer; cryIAb and cryIAc control root-knot nematodes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q13 - Insect-group specificity and acidic gut scenario

questiontext.text: Suppose an insect species has a strongly acidic midgut environment and lacks specific surface receptors on its midgut epithelial cells for a particular Cry protein. What would be the expected outcome if this insect ingests leaves of a Bt crop expressing that Cry protein?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bt toxin crystals require an alkaline gut pH to solubilise and convert from inactive protoxin into active toxin, and the activated toxin must bind to midgut epithelial cell surfaces to form pores.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a strongly acidic gut, the crystals will not solubilise and the protoxin will remain inactive. Furthermore, without binding to midgut epithelial cell surfaces, pore formation, cell swelling, and lysis cannot occur. Hence, the insect will not be killed by the Cry protein.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The protoxin will fail to activate and bind, so the insect will survive without midgut cell lysis.

answer.text: The acidic pH will immediately activate the protoxin and cause rapid lysis of midgut cells
The protoxin will fail to solubilise and activate, and no pore formation or midgut cell lysis will occur
The Cry protein will convert into double-stranded RNA and silence the insect's mRNA
The bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis will colonise the insect gut and kill it via septicaemia

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q14 - Nematode infecting tobacco roots

questiontext.text: Which nematode infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a severe reduction in crop yield, prompting the use of RNA interference (RNAi) for control?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Several nematodes parasitise plants and animals, causing major agricultural losses.

Step 2: Evaluation
Meloidogyne incognita is the nematode that infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield. Bacillus thuringiensis is a bacterium, Agrobacterium is a bacterial vector, and Escherichia coli is a bacterium used in rDNA cloning.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nematode is Meloidogyne incognita.

answer.text: Bacillus thuringiensis
Agrobacterium tumefaciens
Meloidogyne incognita
Escherichia coli

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q15 - Molecular mechanism of RNA interference

questiontext.text: In all eukaryotic organisms, RNA interference (RNAi) functions as a method of cellular defense by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
RNA interference (RNAi) is a post-transcriptional gene-silencing mechanism conserved across eukaryotes.

Step 2: Evaluation
RNAi involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) molecule that binds to the target mRNA and prevents its translation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
RNAi operates by silencing a specific mRNA using a complementary dsRNA molecule that prevents translation.

answer.text: Deleting the target gene directly from the nuclear chromosomal DNA
Methylating all ribosomal RNA subunits inside the nucleolus
Converting single-stranded DNA probes into radioactive fragments
Silencing a specific mRNA via a complementary dsRNA molecule that prevents its translation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q16 - Natural sources of complementary RNA in RNAi

questiontext.text: In nature, what are the potential sources of the complementary RNA that triggers RNA interference (RNAi) as a cellular defense mechanism in eukaryotic organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
RNAi evolved in eukaryotes as an innate defense system against foreign or mobile genetic elements that produce double-stranded RNA intermediates.

Step 2: Evaluation
The source of complementary RNA for RNAi can be either an infection by viruses having RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Complementary RNA in natural RNAi originates from RNA-genome viruses or transposons replicating via an RNA intermediate.

answer.text: Infection by viruses having RNA genomes or transposons replicating via an RNA intermediate
Bacterial plasmids carrying cry genes or mitochondrial DNA
Only retroviral DNA vectors integrated into mammalian lymphocytes
Exclusively chloroplast ribosomal RNA during photosynthesis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q17 - Agrobacterium-mediated sense and anti-sense RNAi in plants

questiontext.text: How does introducing nematode-specific genes via Agrobacterium vectors protect a transgenic tobacco plant from Meloidogyne incognita?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To trigger RNAi against a parasite, the host plant must generate double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) complementary to an essential parasite mRNA.

Step 2: Evaluation
Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific DNA is introduced into the host plant such that it produces both sense and anti-sense RNA in the host cells. Being complementary, these two RNAs form dsRNA, which initiates RNAi and silences the specific mRNA of the nematode, preventing the parasite from surviving in the transgenic host.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The introduced DNA produces both sense and anti-sense RNA that form dsRNA, initiating RNAi and silencing the nematode's specific mRNA.

answer.text: The vector produces Bt protoxin crystals inside the root cortex that lyse nematode gut cells
The introduced DNA produces both sense and anti-sense RNA in host cells, forming dsRNA that silences the nematode's mRNA
The vector induces root gall formation that traps the nematode larvae physically
The introduced DNA synthesises antibodies against nematode surface glycoproteins

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q18 - Approved recombinant therapeutics worldwide and in India

questiontext.text: According to the NCERT textbook, approximately how many recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use worldwide, and how many of these are presently marketed in India?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Recombinant DNA technology enables mass production of safe, effective therapeutic drugs that do not trigger unwanted immunological responses.

Step 2: Evaluation
About 30 recombinant therapeutics have been approved for human use the world over, and 12 of these are presently marketed in India.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Approximately 30 recombinant therapeutics are approved worldwide, with 12 marketed in India.

answer.text: About 12 worldwide and 30 in India
About 50 worldwide and 20 in India
About 30 worldwide and 12 in India
About 100 worldwide and 27 in India

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q19 - Drawback of animal-sourced insulin

questiontext.text: Before the advent of recombinant human insulin, insulin used to treat diabetes was extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs. What was a major drawback of using this animal-derived insulin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Proteins isolated from non-human sources can be recognised as foreign antigens by the human immune system.

Step 2: Evaluation
Insulin isolated from slaughtered cattle and pigs caused some diabetic patients to develop allergies or other unwanted immunological reactions to the foreign protein.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A major drawback of animal-derived insulin was that it caused allergies or other immune reactions to the foreign protein in some patients.

answer.text: It lacked both A and B polypeptide chains
It could only be administered orally rather than by injection
It permanently deleted the patient's own insulin gene
It caused allergies or other reactions to the foreign protein in some patients

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q20 - Structure of mature insulin vs pro-hormone

questiontext.text: How does mature functional human insulin differ structurally from mammalian pro-insulin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as an inactive pro-hormone that must undergo processing to become a fully mature, functional hormone.

Step 2: Evaluation
Pro-insulin contains an extra polypeptide stretch called the C-peptide. During maturation into functional insulin, this C-peptide is removed, leaving only two short polypeptide chains—chain A and chain B—linked together by disulphide bridges.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mature insulin lacks the C-peptide and consists solely of chain A and chain B linked by disulphide bridges.

answer.text: Mature insulin lacks the C-peptide and consists of chains A and B linked by disulphide bridges
Mature insulin retains the C-peptide and lacks disulphide bridges between chains A and B
Mature insulin consists of chains B and C linked by peptide bonds, with chain A removed
Pro-insulin consists of only chain A, whereas mature insulin has chains A, B, and C

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q21 - Eli Lilly recombinant insulin production strategy

questiontext.text: In 1983, how did the American company Eli Lilly successfully produce mature human insulin using recombinant DNA technology?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The primary challenge in producing human insulin via rDNA technology was getting insulin assembled into its mature form without the C-peptide.

Step 2: Evaluation
Eli Lilly prepared two separate DNA sequences corresponding to the A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them into plasmids of E. coli to produce the two chains independently. Chains A and B were then extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Eli Lilly produced chains A and B separately in E. coli plasmids and then extracted and linked them via disulphide bonds.

answer.text: By cloning the entire human pro-insulin gene into Agrobacterium and cleaving C-peptide in tobacco leaves
By introducing separate DNA sequences for chains A and B into E. coli plasmids, producing them separately, and combining them via disulphide bonds
By fusing the C-peptide gene with human alpha-lactalbumin in transgenic cows
By extracting mature insulin from human lymphocytes cultured with retroviral vectors

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q22 - Why insulin cannot be administered orally

questiontext.text: Why can insulin NOT be administered orally to diabetic patients, unlike many small-molecule drugs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Insulin is a peptide hormone composed of two polypeptide chains (chain A and chain B) linked by disulphide bridges.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because insulin is a proteinaceous hormone, if it is taken orally, the proteolytic enzymes (proteases) present in the human digestive tract will digest and break down the polypeptide chains into amino acids before it can be absorbed into the bloodstream in an active form.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Insulin cannot be given orally because it is a protein hormone that gets digested by proteases in the alimentary canal.

answer.text: Insulin is rapidly inactivated by the alkaline pH of the human stomach
Insulin is a nucleic acid that gets degraded by nucleases in saliva
Insulin is a protein hormone that would be digested by proteases in the digestive tract
Oral insulin permanently converts into inactive pro-insulin in the liver

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q23 - First clinical gene therapy in 1990

questiontext.text: The first clinical gene therapy was administered in 1990 to a 4-year-old girl suffering from which genetic disorder?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gene therapy involves delivering a normal, functional gene into a patient's cells or tissues to compensate for a defective or missing gene.

Step 2: Evaluation
In 1990, the first clinical gene therapy was given to a 4-year-old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency, an enzyme crucial for the functioning of the immune system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The first clinical gene therapy treated adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.

answer.text: Phenylketonuria (PKU)
Cystic fibrosis
Emphysema
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q24 - Cause and conventional treatments of ADA deficiency

questiontext.text: ADA deficiency is caused by the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase. Which statement accurately describes the conventional treatments—bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy—for this disorder?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adenosine deaminase (ADA) is an enzyme crucial for the immune system to function, and its deficiency results from deletion of the ADA gene.

Step 2: Evaluation
In some children, ADA deficiency can be treated by bone marrow transplantation, and in others by enzyme replacement therapy (where functional ADA is given by injection). However, the limitation of both approaches is that they are not completely curative.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both bone marrow transplantation and enzyme replacement therapy are not completely curative for ADA deficiency.

answer.text: Both approaches are used to manage the condition, but neither is completely curative
Enzyme replacement therapy provides a permanent genetic cure after a single injection
Bone marrow transplantation uses a retroviral vector to deliver ADA cDNA into embryos
Neither approach can supply functional ADA enzyme to the patient

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q25 - Permanent cure strategy in ADA gene therapy

questiontext.text: In gene therapy for ADA deficiency, why does a patient infused with genetically engineered lymphocytes require periodic infusions, and how could a permanent cure be achieved?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ex vivo gene therapy for ADA deficiency involves culturing patient blood lymphocytes outside the body, introducing functional ADA cDNA using a retroviral vector, and returning the cells to the patient.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because these genetically engineered lymphocytes are not immortal, they eventually die, requiring periodic infusions. However, if the gene isolated from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could provide a permanent cure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Periodic infusions are needed because lymphocytes are not immortal, whereas introducing the ADA gene from marrow cells at early embryonic stages could be a permanent cure.

answer.text: Because retroviral vectors degrade within hours; permanent cure requires oral ADA enzyme tablets
Because lymphocytes are not immortal; permanent cure could be achieved by introducing the ADA gene from marrow cells at early embryonic stages
Because lymphocytes divide uncontrollably; permanent cure requires radiation therapy
Because ADA cDNA cannot be expressed in human cells; permanent cure requires Agrobacterium vectors

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q26 - Early molecular diagnosis using PCR

questiontext.text: Why is Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) superior to conventional serum and urine analysis for diagnosing infectious diseases like HIV in suspected AIDS patients?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Effective disease treatment relies on early diagnosis before pathogen load becomes very high and symptoms appear.

Step 2: Evaluation
Conventional serum and urine analyses generally cannot detect pathogens early, when their concentration is still very low and symptoms are not yet visible. PCR can detect very low concentrations of bacteria or viruses by amplifying their nucleic acid, and is routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients as well as gene mutations in suspected cancer patients.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
PCR enables early detection of very low pathogen concentrations before symptoms appear by amplifying their nucleic acids.

answer.text: PCR directly neutralises viral antigens in the patient's serum
PCR measures antibody titres using enzyme-linked colour reactions
PCR detects very low concentrations of pathogen nucleic acid before symptoms appear by amplifying it
PCR replaces defective alleles in lymphocytes with functional cDNA

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q27 - Radioactive probe hybridisation and autoradiography

questiontext.text: A single-stranded DNA or RNA molecule tagged with a radioactive probe is allowed to hybridise with complementary DNA in a clone of cells, followed by autoradiography. What happens to a clone of cells carrying a mutated gene on the photographic film, and why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acid hybridisation depends on base-pair complementarity between the radioactive single-stranded probe and the target DNA sequence.

Step 2: Evaluation
When a cell clone contains a mutated gene, the sequence alteration means the radioactive probe will not have complementarity with the mutated gene and therefore will not hybridise to it. As a result, the clone having the mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film during autoradiography.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The clone with the mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film because the probe lacks complementarity with the mutated sequence.

answer.text: It appears brighter than normal clones because the mutation attracts more radioactive probe
It appears as a double band because the probe binds both sense and anti-sense mutated strands
It fluoresces green without requiring photographic film
It does not appear on the photographic film because the probe lacks complementarity with the mutated gene

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q28 - Principle and target detection in ELISA

questiontext.text: ELISA (Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay) is a widely used early diagnostic technique. On what principle is it based, and what can it detect to confirm pathogen infection?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
ELISA is an immunological diagnostic assay designed for early detection of diseases.

Step 2: Evaluation
ELISA is based on the principle of antigen–antibody interaction. Infection by a pathogen can be detected either by the presence of pathogen antigens (such as proteins or glycoproteins) or by detecting the antibodies synthesised by the host against the pathogen.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
ELISA is based on antigen–antibody interaction and detects either pathogen antigens or host antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.

answer.text: Antigen–antibody interaction; detects pathogen antigens or antibodies synthesised against the pathogen
DNA–RNA hybridisation; detects only viral RNA genomes
Thermal nucleic acid amplification; detects only mutated host genes
Protoxin solubilisation; detects alkaline pH changes in infected tissues

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q29 - Predominance of mice among transgenic animals

questiontext.text: Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are called transgenic animals. Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals belong to which group?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transgenic animals—including rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows, fish, and mice—have been engineered to carry and express foreign genes for research and medical applications.

Step 2: Evaluation
Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

answer.text: Rabbits
Mice
Sheep
Pigs

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q30 - Transgenic animal models for human diseases

questiontext.text: Transgenic animals serve as models to understand how genes contribute to disease development and to investigate new treatments. For which set of human diseases do transgenic models currently exist according to the chapter?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transgenic animals are specifically designed to study both normal physiology/development (e.g., insulin-like growth factor) and the genetic basis of human diseases.

Step 2: Evaluation
Transgenic models exist for many human diseases such as cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Transgenic models exist for cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's.

answer.text: Malaria, cholera, tuberculosis, and typhoid
Scurvy, rickets, goitre, and beriberi
Cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and Alzheimer's
Sleeping sickness, elephantiasis, ringworm, and amoebiasis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q31 - Biological products from transgenic animals

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about biological products obtained from transgenic animals is INCORRECT?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Transgenic animals can be engineered by introducing genes coding for expensive therapeutic or nutritional human proteins.

Step 2: Evaluation
Human α-1-antitrypsin is produced to treat emphysema, and similar attempts are being made for phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis. In 1997, the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 g/L) containing human alpha-lactalbumin (not α-1-antitrypsin), making it nutritionally more balanced for human babies than natural cow milk.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The statement claiming Rosie's milk contained α-1-antitrypsin instead of human alpha-lactalbumin is incorrect.

answer.text: Human α-1-antitrypsin produced by transgenic animals is used to treat emphysema

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q34 - Basmati rice diversity and 1997 US patent

questiontext.text: How many documented varieties of Basmati rice are grown in India, and how did an American company obtain US patent rights on a 'new' Basmati variety in 1997?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
India possesses one of the richest diversities of rice in the world (an estimated 200,000 varieties), including aromatic Basmati rice documented in ancient texts and folklore.

Step 2: Evaluation
There are 27 documented varieties of Basmati grown in India. In 1997, an American company obtained patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office by crossing Indian Basmati with semi-dwarf varieties and claiming the resulting variety as a novelty or invention.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
India has 27 documented Basmati varieties, and the 1997 US patent was obtained by crossing Indian Basmati with semi-dwarf varieties.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q35 - Definition of biopiracy and Indian herbal examples

questiontext.text: What does the term 'biopiracy' refer to, and which Indian traditional herbal medicines have also faced unauthorised patenting attempts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Indigenous communities and developing nations possess rich biodiversity and traditional knowledge that can be exploited commercially without fair benefit sharing.

Step 2: Evaluation
Biopiracy refers to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned and without compensatory payment. Besides Basmati rice, several attempts have been made to patent uses, products, and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines such as turmeric and neem.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Biopiracy is the unauthorised use of bio-resources without compensatory payment, and turmeric and neem are traditional Indian examples targeted by patent attempts.

answer.text: Illegal smuggling of genetically modified seeds across borders; golden rice and Bt cotton
Authorised commercial licensing of microbial enzymes; insulin and ADA
Deliberate release of nematode pests into crop fields; tobacco and potato
Use of bio-resources by multinational companies without proper authorisation and compensatory payment; turmeric and neem

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CH12_MCQ_Q36 - Biodiversity disparity and Indian Patents Bill amendment

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately contrasts industrialised nations with developing nations regarding bio-resources, and describes India's legislative response to biopiracy?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Global debates on biopiracy highlight the imbalance between financial capital and biological/traditional wealth, prompting national legal protections.

Step 2: Evaluation
Most industrialised nations are financially rich but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, whereas developing and underdeveloped nations are rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources. To counter unauthorised exploitation and inadequate benefit sharing, the Indian Parliament cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill, taking into consideration patent terms, emergency provisions, and research and development initiatives.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Industrialised nations are financially rich but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge, while developing nations are rich in both; India addressed this through the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill.

answer.text: Industrialised nations are financially rich but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge; India cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill covering patent terms, emergency provisions, and R&D initiatives
Industrialised nations are rich in both finance and biodiversity; India abolished all patent laws to prevent biopiracy
Developing nations are poor in traditional knowledge; India delegated all patent decisions to the US Patent and Trademark Office
Developing nations are financially rich and poor in biodiversity; India passed the first amendment of the GEAC Act to ban GM crops
